title: M-Ch-L

segments.voice: Yesterday, S-L-Ch: selichah, pardon, and slicha, excuse me. Your line was forgive. Which small thing did you pardon, and did it stay pardoned? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-three.

A friend borrowed some cash in the spring. It's autumn now. Neither of you mentions it, and both of you remember it every time you split a check. There are three ways this ends. Somebody pays. Somebody nags. Or the lender says, out loud, forget it, we're square, and means it. That third ending has a name in the language of the rabbis. Mechilah. It's the word a court would use for waiving a claim, and it's the word Jews use, especially before Yom Kippur, when they ask one another for forgiveness. Today's root: mem, chet, lamed. M-Ch-L.
screen: `A DEBT NOBODY MENTIONS.` → `PAY, NAG, OR WAIVE.` → `M-CH-L: TO WAIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's root, S-L-Ch, was pardon. Today's is quieter and more practical. Mechilah is the word for giving up something you're owed. Turn it four ways. First, the ledger. In the rabbis' legal language, if someone owes you and you say machul lach, it's waived, the debt is gone. Nobody pays it back. You simply stop holding the paper. Second, the question. Two days ago, K-P-R brought the Mishnah's line that between people, Yom Kippur waits until they make peace. Mechilah is the name for what one person asks the other in that moment. Not, do you feel better? Not, was it fine? Will you waive it? Friends, siblings, coworkers, asking each other one plain question before the fast. Third, the asker's side. The Talmud discusses what to do when the person you hurt won't grant it, and teaches that you keep trying, sincerely and with others present, but there is a limit. Asking for forgiveness is a duty. Forcing it is not. Fourth, the night. In traditional prayer books, the Shema said at bedtime opens with a short paragraph in which a person declares that they forgive anyone who wronged them, in word or in deed. Every night, a small mechilah before sleep. Look back at this week and the roots line up: calling out, books, aiming, missing the mark, covering, pardon, and now waiving. One week, one long walk from what's written to what's owed.
screen: `THE LEDGER: MACHUL, IT'S WAIVED.` · `THE QUESTION: WILL YOU WAIVE IT?` · `THE ASKER: ASK, DON'T FORCE.` · `THE NIGHT: FORGIVEN BEFORE SLEEP.` · then, large: `מְחִילָה`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let one debt go. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something someone owes you. Money, maybe. Or an apology, a returned favor, a call they never made. Hold it the way a lender holds a note. Notice how long you have been carrying it. Then try the bedtime words in your own voice, silently: whatever this person owes me, I let it go. You don't have to tell them. You don't have to pretend it was fine. Just put the paper down. If you pray, you can bring their name into the quiet. The bell holds the time.
M-Ch-L. Mem, chet, lamed: the root of mechilah, waiving what you're owed, and the forgiveness Jews ask of one another before Yom Kippur. Today's word.
Your line: let it go. Tonight, before you sleep, waive one thing someone owes you, and notice whether you sleep any lighter. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Before Yom Kippur, Jews traditionally seek out people they may have wronged and ask for mechilah, forgiveness, and traditional prayer books include a declaration of forgiveness for others at the start of the bedtime Shema.

myth: mechilah means the debt gets paid back in full
it means the one who is owed stops holding the claim. nobody pays it back.

original.note: Hebrew: waiving a claim; forgiveness between people.

trapdoor: what you thought: forgiveness is a feeling that happens to you.
what it means: mechilah is waiving a debt, a choice to stop holding what you're owed.
what a scholar hears: Yoma 87a — ask sincerely, with others present, but there is a limit; and the bedtime Shema opens with forgiving others.

notes: The Talmud's limit on how many times to ask (Yoma 87a; codified as three times by Maimonides, Hilchot Teshuvah 2:9) is described without a number; confirm the summary.
'Machul lach' as the idiom for a waived claim: confirm phrasing and gender form (lach/lecha).
'Many prayer books' include the forgiveness paragraph (Ribbono shel olam, hareini mochel) at the bedtime Shema; confirm this is fair across communities.
The hook's loan is an invented everyday scene, not a source claim.
